**Title:** Which Dollar Broke? Separating Token Failures from Platform-Ledger Failures in Web Dollar Markets

**Abstract (298 words):**

Crypto prices on the Web are quoted in two kinds of dollar: stablecoin tokens, and balances in an exchange's internal ledger that reach the banking system only through the platform's rails. Price feeds and oracles average these quotes as if every USD quote were in the same dollar, and we know of no measure that tells a token failure from a ledger failure. This is hard because a ledger's value is never quoted directly, public prices are asynchronous last trades that thin out under stress, and any single asset may carry its own shock. We price the platform's dollar through unpegged assets against venues whose rails stay open, which splits a dollar-quoted dislocation into a token and a ledger component, and we accept the split only when unrelated assets agree and the venue's internal cross-rates hold. We study rail-cut episodes on three platforms: three Bitfinex windows from 2017 to 2019, Binance.US in 2023, and Binance's sterling and euro rails. On Bitfinex and Binance.US the platform's dollar, not a token, moved: by up to 844 bps on Bitfinex, with BTC and ETH agreeing to within 7.2 bps and internal cross-rates holding to within 8 bps. On both platforms it traded at a discount while exit was impaired and later at a premium. A volume-weighted BTC/USD index over these venues was off by at least 100 bps for 2,826 hours; dropping the venue-hours our rule flags removes 88% of them. On Bitfinex in 2018 the discount appeared 3 days before the deposit freeze was first reported and about 6.5 months before regulators disclosed the loss behind it. In the March 2023 USDC run, by contrast, the method attributes all but 6% of the dislocation to the token. The sterling and euro cuts show only small effects. All findings are descriptive.

**Suggested keywords:** stablecoins; platform money; exchange ledgers; price feeds and oracles; Web measurement; natural experiment; reproducibility
